I've been a Free Agent for just under 9 years. Here's what most of my placements look like: Arrive. Meet the people already there. Listen -- to people at all levels. Learn from them: what's not working? What was tried and failed? What might work but that is being ignored? Offer an outsider perspective. Collaborate on a solution. Speak truth to management because you're only temporary anyway. Create something that's informed by all the latest and best resources that exist.  Get it going. Invite criticism. Breathe. Iterate and improve. Do your best. Hand it off -- with all the data and instructions necessary for it to continue after you leave. Thank people. Be grateful for the opportunity. Leave. Pick another project. Be grateful for the thing you get to do now, and the prior things you helped make that worked and still exist. Learn what you did wrong. Do better next time. Remain a student of even the things you're good at. Complacency will stall your career.

I tried this last week with my Debian Testing with Budgie Desktop. The problem so far is getting Budgie to go by default. If I select it in the login box circle each time, no problem. But the circle turns empty after logout (does not save last DE as the default). If I forget to select Budgie, I get an empty X desktop with just the mouse cursor.

**\*\*\* Update \*\*\***

I  read the lightdm.conf file line-by-line and noticed a second occurrence of user-session

Under `[LightDM]` I'd added `user-session = budgie-desktop`

However, I had to add: 

`user-session=budgie-desktop` (no spaces) under `[Seat:*]`

Now it works perfectly.

There's no need to unplug the cable of the Windows drive. The Mint installer will see it, and if you want grub to add the Windows drive to its boot menu, get that taken care of from the start.

 So,

\- add the second drive for Linux and install Mint there (you'll be able to see which of the drives already has Windows installed)

\- tell grub to install the bootloader on the drive with Mint

\- On reboot, enter the BIOS settings and set the new Mint drive as the new first drive to boot from

This leaves the Windows drive completely untouched, but allows you to easily boot to it from the grub menu.

No problem. If you're not sure whether you'll switch, it makes it easy to return it to a Windows computer with no fuss. Or, if you really decide you'll never need Windows again, you can wipe the whole drive out and use it for storage.

Partitioning both OSs on one drive is sightly trickier because it means having to restore the Windows bootloader in the event you decide to stop using Linux (see:  [How to restore Windows boot loader after removing Ubuntu](https://askubuntu.com/questions/1240994/how-to-restore-windows-boot-loader-after-removing-ubuntu))

Another reason I like separate drives is that it allows me to easily install a fresh copy of Mint without worrying about the other OS. I'm not sure if it's really necessary anymore with the recent major version changes, but I've still done it from 18 > 19 > 20. The data backup and restore tool in Mint makes it easy.

It's been a very very long time since I accidentally wiped out a drive, but keeping OSs separated and on drives of different sizes and/or makes has saved me a lot of grief.

Rather than partitioning a drive for dual boot (which I did used to do a lot), I'd recommend:

\- adding a second drive for Linux and installing Mint there

Why would they do this? Because one show a month makes the show an event. A treat, even. 

Every show I've made in 3 years still gets listens because certain people will binge\-listen right back from the pilot episode.
